summary: Defines an XML format extension for representing copy control attributes in resource lists. When a SIP request is sent to a group of recipients through a server, the list of URIs is carried as a resource list XML document. The extension marks whether each recipient is addressed directly, copied, or blind-copied. It has been updated since.

eli5.summary: Like To, Cc and Bcc in email, this lets a group message mark who is the main recipient, who is copied, and who is secretly copied.

questions: xml extension for to cc bcc in resource list
what is copycontrol in sip resource lists
how does sip support bcc recipients
subtitle: To, Cc and Bcc for SIP group requests: labelling each recipient in an XML resource list.

tldr.problem: When one SIP request is sent to a server that fans it out to a list of recipients, the XML resource list has no way to say who is a primary recipient, who is copied and who is blind-copied.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a copyControl attribute (to, cc, bcc), an anonymize attribute and a count attribute to resource list entries, and defines how the URI-list server builds a recipient-history list from them.
tldr.outcome: Recipients can see who else got the request, while bcc recipients stay hidden and anonymized ones are shown only as a count. RFC 5364 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5364 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why Copy Control Is Needed
sections.content:
A URI-list service receives one SIP request that contains a list of URIs and sends a similar request to each URI in the list. The list is normally an XML resource list as defined in RFC 4826, and it can appear both in the request sent to the server and in each request the server sends on.

The resource list format lacks a way to say whether a recipient gets a primary copy, a carbon copy or a blind carbon copy. This document adds that, as in email where each recipient is a "to", "cc" or "bcc". It also lets the sender ask that some recipients' URIs be anonymized, so they are not disclosed to the other recipients.
sections.eli5: When one message goes to many people, it helps to say who it is mainly for, who is just getting a copy, and who is secretly getting one.

sections.title: How the Server Uses the Lists
sections.content:
The sender puts a recipient list in the request to the URI-list server. Each target can carry a copyControl attribute. When the server expands the request, it builds a recipient-history list and puts it in each outgoing request in place of the recipient list. That list shows the visible recipients: the "to" and "cc" entries are copied across and "bcc" entries are left out.

A recipient can then see which other visible recipients got the request and whether each is "to" or "cc", and can reply to them.

The anonymize attribute differs from "bcc". A bcc recipient is removed, so others do not notice that anyone else received the request. An anonymized recipient is replaced by an anonymous URI, so others see that extra recipients exist but not who they are.
sections.eli5: The server writes a guest list for each person that leaves out the secret guests. Anonymous guests show up as "some people" with a number.

sections.title: The Three New Attributes
sections.content:
The extension adds attributes to the <entry> element of the resource list format, and they SHOULD be usable on any child element of <list>, such as <external>. The schema in Section 5 uses the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol.

  • copyControl: one of "to", "cc" or "bcc". If it is absent it MUST be treated as "bcc".
  • anonymize: a boolean, default "false". When true, the server can route to the URI but MUST convert it to sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid in recipient-history lists.
  • count: the number of equal URIs, default "1". It is mainly expected on grouped anonymous entries in recipient-history lists.
sections.eli5: There are three little labels you can stick on a name: how they get the message, whether to hide their name, and how many hidden names are grouped together.

sections.title: Processing Rules for the Server
sections.content:
The server MUST treat "bcc" URIs in one of two ways. It removes all bcc URIs from the recipient-history list, so every recipient gets the same list but bcc recipients are not told. Or it keeps only the URI that identifies the recipient being sent to and removes the other bcc URIs, so each recipient gets a different list and bcc recipients are explicitly informed.

If a URI appears more than once, that is an error, and the server should send at most one copy to that recipient. It MUST pick the highest precedence copyControl value, in the order "to", "cc", "bcc".

A "bcc" value takes precedence over anonymize: the URI is removed and the anonymize attribute is ignored. So anonymize is only useful with "to" and "cc".

Receiving implementations SHOULD stop the user from replying to all recipients when their own URI is missing from the recipient-history list or is tagged "bcc". Otherwise, the existence of blind recipients would be revealed.
sections.eli5: If the same name is on the list twice, the server keeps the most visible label. And if you were secretly copied, your mail program should not let you hit reply-all and spill the secret.

sections.title: Worked Example and Carrying Lists in SIP
sections.content:
The RFC's example recipient list has seven entries: three "to" (two of them anonymized), two "cc" (one anonymized) and two "bcc". The server creates seven SIP requests. The recipient-history list sent to each keeps bill and joe, replaces the two anonymized "to" entries with one sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid entry with count 2, replaces the anonymized "cc" entry with one with count 1, and drops both bcc entries.

In SIP, the sender labels its list body with a Content-Disposition of recipient-list, as set out in RFC 5363. This RFC registers a new disposition type, recipient-list-history, for the list the server sends out. The server SHOULD add a handling parameter set to "optional", so recipients that do not support this specification do not reject the request. Legacy recipients that cannot handle multipart bodies cannot be sent a request that also needs another body.
sections.eli5: Seven people are invited, but each guest only sees a short list: the open names, plus "2 other people" and "1 other person" for the hidden ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST follow the security rules of RFC 5363, which include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients. URI lists may hold private information, so it is RECOMMENDED to encrypt list bodies with S/MIME or to protect the SIP request with TLS.

A URI list does not prove who took part. It only names the URIs invited, and it can be spoofed. Mishandling bcc can leak confidential information, for example when a blind recipient replies to all. With the second bcc method, a list that contains all the bcc URIs would show every bcc recipient to every other one.
sections.eli5: The list is only a list of invitations, not proof anyone came, and care is needed so that secret names are not leaked by accident.

items.label: Blind carbon copy
items.desc: Removed from the recipient-history list. This is the default when the attribute is absent.

data.title: Recipient-history list
data.code:
<resource-lists xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists"
          xmlns:cp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol">
  <list>
    <entry uri="sip:bill@example.com" cp:copyControl="to" />
    <entry uri="sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid" cp:copyControl="to"
                                                 cp:count="2"/>
    <entry uri="sip:joe@example.org" cp:copyControl="cc" />
    <entry uri="sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid" cp:copyControl="cc"
                                                 cp:count="1"/>
  </list>
</resource-lists>
